learning_outcomes.text: The course aims at providing students with the basic knowledge of chemistry essential for understanding the relationships between microscopic structure of matter and macroscopic properties of materials which are essential for addressing the interpretation of chemical-physical phenomena typical of electronic engineering.

Knowledge and understanding of the mathematical principles and experimental sciences underlying engineering (e.g., knowledge and understanding of the fundamental models and laws of chemistry relevant to electronic engineering).

Knowledge and understanding of the fundamental principles of chemistry, the chemical-structural characteristics of matter, and the basics of thermochemistry (e.g., the relationships between chemical composition, microscopic structure, and the macroscopic properties of materials, with particular reference to electrical properties; the transformations of matter).

Applying logical-mathematical analysis methodologies to the study of other scientific-technological disciplines (e.g., the ability to solve mono-disciplinary chemistry problems using the proposed models and laws).

Extrapolating application-oriented information from analytical results to be used in the study of engineering problems (e.g., the ability to predict the relationships between chemical composition/microscopic structure of matter and the macroscopic properties of materials (including the transformations they may undergo)).
Writing and balancing chemical equations, performing stoichiometric calculations.

Identifying appropriate calculation methods, procedures for collecting and processing information (measurements, experimental results, laboratory activity outcomes, etc.), and interpreting the resulting data, also through statistical analysis.

Selecting relevant information in a specific context and formulating independent yet rigorous and technically sound judgements, including reflection on any social, scientific, or ethical issues related to them. (e.g., the ability to identify and critically and independently evaluate the chemical and physical transformations of matter, as well as its properties, linking them to its microscopic characteristics).

Appropriately preparing for subsequent levels of education (Master's degrees) (e.g., the ability to read, consult, and understand a scientific text or document with chemistry content. Utilizing the fundamental chemistry knowledge acquired to approach the study of subsequent disciplines requiring basic knowledge of chemistry).

syllabus_topics: Atoms, ions and molecules
Electronic structure of atoms and chemical periodicity
Chemical bonding and molecular structure
Intermolecular forces and states of matter
Solid state. Classification of solids by type of attraction of units
Chemical equations and reaction stoichiometry
Electrochemistry. Voltaic cells and cell potential. Some commercial voltaic cells. Corrosion. Electrolytic cells. Stoichiometry of electrolysis
Electrons in solids
The atomic model of matter; subatomic particles; atomic weight, molecular weight, isotopes, mole

The electromagnetic radiation; the atomic spectra; the black body radiation and the photoelectric effect; the wave-particle duality and De Broglie's relationship; the Heisenberg uncertainty principle; the wave function; the Schrodinger equation; the particle in the box; the quantization of energy; energy levels; the atomic orbitals and the quantum numbers; the wave function in polar coordinates and its meaning
The polyelectronic atoms; the quantum number of spin; the Aufbau principle
The periodic table of the elements; periodic quantities
Introduction to chemical bonding. The covalent bond; the geometry of molecules (VSEPR theory); VB theory, resonance; pure and polar covalent bonds; dipole moment; polar and apolar molecules
Introduction to Molecular Orbitals and Band theories. Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors (valence bond vs band theory models)
Conductive polymers (elements)
The ionic bond
General characteristics of metals and metallic bond (gas electron theory)

Intermolecular forces and states of aggregation of matter. The solid state: amorphous solids and crystalline solids. Crystalline lattices and elementary cells. Types of solids and related properties: metallic, ionic, covalent and molecular. Allotropy, polymorphism and isomorphism. Crystal defects (elements)
Gaseous state and ideal gas law equation. Gas mixtures. Real gases
State diagrams
Chemical reactions. Reactions in solution (molarity and pH). Oxidation-reduction reactions; oxidation number, balancing redox reactions

Electrochemistry. Voltaic cells; the Nernst equation; spontaneity and displacement of redox reactions; oxidation-reduction reactions of water; electrolysis of molten salts and in aqueous solution; Faraday laws. Commercial Voltaic cells. The phenomenon of corrosion. Strategies for corrosion protection
assessment_rules: The student evaluation includes a written exam which, if passed, gives access to the oral exam. Passing the written exam is a prerequisite for the oral exam. The final grade is expressed as a final score. A final grade of 18-22 indicates sufficient knowledge, while 29-30 cum laude represents excellent or outstanding knowledge, with honors awarded for brilliance and originality.
